papers.title_in_file: Gaussian Boson Sampling for binary optimization
papers.what_it_is: A short IEEE conference paper that uses a Gaussian Boson Sampler ansatz with a CVaR-VQE cost to solve a small Flight Gate Assignment problem in simulation.

assertions.value: The authors report that, in numerical simulations on randomly generated Flight Gate Assignment instances, a Gaussian Boson Sampler ansatz trained with a CVaR cost outperforms plain VQE significantly, reaching almost perfect success rates for most of the parameter settings tested.
quotes: We observe that employing CVaR outperforms VQE signif
achieving almost perfect success rates for
assertions.certainty_reason: One simulation study on small random instances.
assertions.reader_inference: The comparison is between CVaR-VQE and plain VQE on the same GBS ansatz. It is not a comparison with a classical optimizer.

assertions.value: The authors state that the work focuses on small-sized instances and serves as an initial proof of principle for the approach.
quotes: Despite focusing on small-sized instances, this work serves as an initial proof of principle for this new approach.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state their own scope in the Conclusion, Section VII, p.2.

assertions.value: The authors report that for one setting of the CVaR parameter and the larger problem sizes tested, the fraction of successful runs decreases, that the failing instances typically involve 3 or 4 flight activities, and that the algorithm appears trapped in local minima.
quotes: the failing instances typically involve 3 or 4 flight activities. The algorithm appears here to be trapped in local minima.
assertions.certainty_reason: One simulation study; the local-minima cause is the authors' reading.

papers.title_in_file: Exploring Quantum Neural Networks for the Discovery and Implementation of Quantum Error-Correcting Codes
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, introduction, bit-flip results and limitations, amplitude damping and code-discovery sections skimmed, conclusions. Appendix not read.
papers.what_it_is: A simulation study that trains dissipative quantum neural networks and quantum autoencoders to perform bit-flip and amplitude-damping error correction and to discover a bit-flip code.

assertions.value: The authors report that they implement the Bit-Flip quantum error-correcting code with a Quantum Autoencoder, which corrects bit-flip errors in arbitrary logical qubit states.
quotes: we successfully implement the Bit-Flip quantum error-correcting code using a Quantum Autoencoder, demonstrating its ability to correct bit-flip errors in arbitrary logical qubit states
assertions.certainty_reason: Simulated result from one study.
assertions.reader_inference: The result concerns a known code that is built into the autoencoder task, not a new code.

assertions.value: The authors state that their results indicate that modified dissipative quantum neural networks outperform default implementations across all tasks considered in the paper.
quotes: Our results indicate that modified DQNNs outperform default implementations across all tasks considered in this work.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one study.

assertions.value: The authors state that if more than two bit flip errors occur, the autoencoder may fail to identify and correct the error, and that their models are sub-optimal algorithms.
assertions.anchor: Section 4, Limitations of this Approach, p.8
quotes: if more than two bit flip errors occur, the QAE may fail to accurately identify and correct the error
Although the QAE models developed in this work are sub-optimal algorithms
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state their own limit in Section 4, Limitations of this Approach.

papers.partial_detail: Abstract, introduction, results (circuit and noise sections), discussion, limitations, conclusion. Methods details skimmed.
papers.what_it_is: A genetic-algorithm architecture search for quantum SVM feature maps restricted to IBM Torino native gates, tested on one UCI breast cancer dataset.

assertions.value: The authors report that the hardware-aware search discovers a 12-gate circuit using exclusively IBM native gates that achieves 91.23% accuracy on 10 qubits on the UCI Breast Cancer Wisconsin dataset, approaching the classical RBF SVM baseline (93%).
quotes: discovers a 12-gate circuit using exclusively IBM
achieves 91.23% accuracy on 10 qubits
approaches classical RBF SVM baseline (93%)
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one study on one dataset.
assertions.reader_inference: The 91.23% figure is described as the noise-free baseline, so it comes from a noise-free simulation. The text read does not report a run on IBM hardware.

assertions.value: The authors report a 27 percentage point improvement over hand-crafted quantum feature maps (64% accuracy).
quotes: This represents a 27 percentage point improvement over hand-crafted quantum feature maps (64% accuracy)
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one study.

assertions.value: The authors report that the noise-resilient search variant achieves 70.18% accuracy under noise models of 1% single-qubit depolarizing, 2% two-qubit depolarizing and 0.5% amplitude damping, compared with the noise-free 91.23% baseline.
quotes: The noise-resilient NAS variant achieves 70.18% accuracy under realistic noise models (1% single-qubit depolarizing, 2% two-qubit depolarizing, 0.5% amplitude damping), showing relatively graceful degradation compared to the noise-free 91.23% baseline.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one study.
assertions.reader_inference: The drop from 91.23% to 70.18% is a loss of more than 20 points under the stated noise, which the authors call relatively graceful.

assertions.value: The authors state that the results are specific to the Breast Cancer dataset, that the experiments used populations of 8 genomes over 4 generations, and that the circuits tested are far from the regime where quantum advantage might emerge.
quotes: These results are specific to the Breast Cancer dataset.
Our experiments used populations of 8 genomes over 4 generations, representing a modest exploration of the architecture space.
but far from the regime where quantum advantage might emerge
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors list these limits in Section IV.E, Limitations.

papers.title_in_file: A Mixture-of-Experts Framework for Practical Hybrid-Quantum Models in Credit Card Fraud Detection
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, introduction, model and router sections, experiments, results tables, discussion. Reference list and equation details skimmed.
papers.what_it_is: An Oxford Quantum Circuits and Mastercard study that routes a small share of credit card transactions to a hybrid quantum-classical model and the rest to XGBoost.

assertions.value: The authors report an average precision of 0.793 for the routed hybrid architecture at a router threshold of 0.6, against 0.770 for XGBoost, on 3 repeated 5-fold cross-validation benchmarks on a European credit card dataset.
quotes: the routed hybrid architecture with 0.6 threshold achieves average precision scores of 0.793
compared to 0.770
XGBoost on 3 repeated 5-fold cross-validation benchmarks
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one study on one public dataset.
assertions.reader_inference: The reported spreads are about 0.085 and 0.096, so the 0.023 gap is small against them. The authors call the gain marginal in the Table 5 caption.

assertions.value: The authors report that the hybrid model achieves lower recall than XGBoost, a precision and recall trade-off in which false positives fall at the cost of missing a small fraction of additional fraud cases.
quotes: our model achieves lower recall than XGBoost, indicating a precision/recall trade-off
the hybrid model reduces false positives at the cost of missing a small fraction of additional fraud cases
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one study.

assertions.value: The authors report that about 3% of holdout points sent to quantum hardware added an additional inference overhead of 21 minutes in the worst case, while a fully quantum architecture on a holdout set of approximately 14,000 points would require nearly 12 hours for inference alone.
quotes: the holdout set contained approximately 14,000 points, implying that a fully quantum architecture would require nearly 12 hours for inference alone
approximately 3% of the points were submitted to quantum hardware, resulting in an additional inference overhead of 21 minutes
assertions.certainty_reason: Timing result from one study on one hardware device.
assertions.reader_inference: The text says hardware clock time was obtained for 10 points, so the 12 hour figure looks like an extrapolation from those timings and not a full run.

assertions.value: The authors state that the evaluation uses a European credit card dataset in which roughly 0.172% of the data is classified as fraud, and that the Time column was removed.

Since we opted to use cross-validation in our benchmark, we decided to remove the

papers.title_in_file: Efficient Postprocessing Procedure for Evaluating Hamiltonian Expectation Values in Variational Quantum Eigensolver
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, introduction, results text, conclusions, complexity appendix skimmed.
papers.what_it_is: A classical postprocessing speedup for VQE that stores the eigenvalue of each measured bit string in a dictionary (measurement memory) so repeated bit strings are not re-evaluated.

assertions.value: The authors state that they analyze the complexity of the measurement memory procedure, compare it with the commonly used postprocessing procedure, and find that it is always more efficient in terms of time complexity.
quotes: We further analyze the complexity of MM and compare it with commonly employed post-processing procedure, finding that MM is always more efficient in terms of time complexity.
assertions.certainty_reason: Analytic comparison summarized in the abstract; the appendix proof was only skimmed.

assertions.value: The authors report that, for a fully connected Ising Hamiltonian up to 20 qubits where all O(N 2) terms commute, the method offers an O(N 2) speedup in terms of the percentage of time saved.
quotes: For Ising Hamiltonian, where all O(N 2) terms commute, our method offers an O(N 2) speedup in terms of the percentage of time saved.
minimizing a fully connected Ising Hamiltonians up to 20 qubits
assertions.certainty_reason: Simulation result from one study.
assertions.reader_inference: The speedup is in classical postprocessing time, not in the number of circuit repetitions.

assertions.value: The authors state that for the Fermion grouping case the qubit sizes they can demonstrate are at the transition point of the term scaling, which makes the improvement harder to estimate for larger systems.
quotes: the qubit sizes we are able to demonstrate here are at the transition point of the term scaling
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state this limit in the results discussion of Section IV, p.3.

papers.title_in_file: Provably faster randomized and quantum algorithms for k-means clustering via uniform sampling
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, introduction with contributions and comparison table, theorem statements, QRAM section headers. Appendix proofs not read.
papers.what_it_is: A JPMorganChase theory paper that gives a uniform-sampling mini-batch k-means algorithm and a QRAM-based quantum analogue with improved worst-case bounds.

assertions.value: The authors state that they describe a simple randomized mini-batch k-means algorithm and an inspired quantum algorithm, that their worst case guarantees can significantly improve on the bounds in prior work, and that the improvement is due to a careful use of uniform sampling, which preserves symmetries of the k-means problem that data norm-based sampling does not.
quotes: In this work, we describe a simple randomized mini-batch k-means algorithm and a quantum algorithm inspired by the classical algorithm.
We demonstrate that the worst case guarantees of these algorithms can significantly improve upon the bounds for algorithms in prior work.

Our improvements are due to a careful use of uniform sampling, which preserves certain symmetries of the k-means problem that are not preserved in previous algorithms that use data norm-based sampling.
assertions.certainty_reason: Theorem 2.1 and Corollary 2.2, Section 2, give the classical bound.
assertions.reader_inference: The bounds are worst-case guarantees; no runtime experiment is reported in the text read.

assertions.value: The authors state that, assuming superposition quantum access to the data using QRAM, they show a quadratic improvement in one parameter dependence over their classical algorithm in the small-parameter regime, and that the quantum algorithm will do better than the classical algorithm only when that parameter is small.
quotes: Assuming superposition quantum access to the data using QRAM
we showcase a quadratic improvement in the
the quantum algorithm will do better than the classical algorithm when
assertions.certainty_reason: Theorem 3.5, Section 3, gives the QRAM query bound.
assertions.reader_inference: The advantage is conditional on QRAM and a small-parameter regime.

assertions.value: The authors state that the main result holds if the initial clusters are roughly balanced, and that their quantum guarantee is stated as QRAM query complexity, not time complexity.
quotes: Our main result is that, if the initial clusters are roughly balanced
because the authors analyze time complexity, whereas our study focuses on QRAM query complexity
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state the balanced-cluster assumption and the query-complexity measure in Section 1.2.

papers.title_in_file: SAFE Quantum Machine Learning with Variational Quantum Classifiers
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, introduction, methodology summary, data and evaluation protocol, results sections 4.3.1 to 4.3.5, conclusions, impact statement. Appendix not read.
papers.what_it_is: A study of a 9-qubit variational quantum classifier on ResNet-18 features of brain tumor MRI images, compared with classical models on accuracy, robustness and explainability metrics.

assertions.value: The authors report a mean F1-macro score of 0.978 for the variational quantum model and 0.983 for the SVM, the highest among the classical baselines, in 5-fold cross-validation.
quotes: The proposed QML model achieved a mean F1-macro score of 0.978
SVM achieved the highest mean F1-macro score (0.983
All models are evaluated using 5-fold cross-validation.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one study on one dataset.
assertions.reader_inference: The QML model ran on a simulator and the SVM scored higher.

assertions.value: The authors report that the quantum model achieves the highest robustness to Gaussian input perturbations (AURGR), and that the Random Forest provides the strongest explainability stability (AURGE).
quotes: the QML achieves the highest robustness to Gaussian input perturbations (AURGR), and the Random Forest provides the strongest explainability stability (AURGE)
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one study.
assertions.reader_inference: Table 3 gives AURGR as 0.9409 with a spread of 0.0013 for QML and 0.9393 with a spread of 0.0052 for SVM, so the two overlap.

assertions.value: The authors state that the quantum component was executed on a noiseless quantum simulator, that they deliberately do not report computational time comparisons, and that the circuit is a single Strongly Entangling Layer acting on 9 qubits.
assertions.anchor: Section 6 Impact statement, p.23; Section 3.1, p.5
quotes: with the quantum component executed on a noiseless quantum simulator
a single Strongly Entangling Layer acting on 9 qubits
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state the simulator setting in Section 6 and the circuit in Section 3.1.

assertions.value: The authors state that the value of the proposed quantum model lies not in surpassing classical methods in peak accuracy but in providing a compact, structured hypothesis class that supports SAFE learning objectives.
quotes: the value of the proposed quantum model lies not in surpassing classical methods in peak accuracy
assertions.certainty_reason: Author interpretation in the Conclusions.

papers.title_in_file: Quantum State Learning Implies Circuit Lower Bounds
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, introduction, theorem statements, proof overview, discussion and open questions. Formal proofs in later sections and appendices not read.
papers.what_it_is: A complexity theory paper that shows sufficiently efficient state tomography or distinguishing from Haar random would imply circuit lower bounds for state synthesis and decision problems.

assertions.value: The authors state that they establish connections between state tomography, pseudorandomness, quantum state synthesis, and circuit lower bounds, and that even slightly non-trivial quantum state tomography algorithms would lead to new statements about quantum state synthesis.
quotes: We establish connections between state tomography, pseudorandomness, quantum state synthesis, and circuit lower bounds.
we show that even slightly non-trivial quantum state tomography algorithms would lead to new statements about quantum state synthesis
assertions.certainty_reason: Theorem 1.1, stated formally as Corollary 6.5.

assertions.value: The authors state that a slight modification of their proof shows that distinguishing algorithms for quantum states can imply circuit lower bounds for decision problems as well.
quotes: a slight modification of our proof shows that distinguishing algorithms for quantum states can imply circuit lower bounds for decision problems as well
assertions.certainty_reason: Theorem 1.3, stated formally as Theorem A.4.

assertions.value: The authors state that the lower bound holds regardless of how efficient the learning algorithm is, as long as it is more efficient than a certain threshold, and that a stronger lower bound from a polynomial-time or quasi-polynomial-time learner is left as a wish for future work.
assertions.anchor: Section 1.3, Discussion and Open Questions, p.11
quotes: This bound holds regardless of how efficient the learning algorithm is, as long as it is more efficient than a certain threshold.
it would be great if a poly-time (or quasi-poly) learning algorithm implied a stronger lower bound
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state this limit in Section 1.3.
